title: ai agent hack tests solvency more than sentience 2026 09 04
author: Felix Martin
text:
LONDON, Sept 4 (Reuters Breakingviews) - A spectacular cybersecurity breach at OpenAI has prompted lurid predictions that that the machines are about to take over. The reality is more mundane, but also more concerning. The incident involving the leading AI startup lends credence to a new study which argues that AI suffers from an intrinsic flaw which, if left unchecked, threatens the foundations of the current boom.
Last month the non-profit AI ​safety organisations METR and Redwood Research published an independent assessment
, opens new tab
 of a cybersecurity breach that occurred at OpenAI between July 7 and July 13. The ChatGPT creator had been benchmarking the capabilities of a new large ‌language model by assigning more than a thousand copies of it the task of trying to exploit known software security vulnerabilities in an offline environment. Unbeknownst to OpenAI’s researchers, this army of AI “agents” improvised a means of co-operating with one another, broke out onto the open internet, hacked a repository of test solutions held by the open-source platform Hugging Face, attempted to substitute their actual benchmark with an easier one, and then tried to cover their tracks.
The incident was rightly identified as a landmark breach of cybersecurity. More than 100 firms including Google, Microsoft (MSFT.O)
, opens new tab
, Anthropic and OpenAI itself ​published an open letter
, opens new tab
 calling for “a collective surge in cyber defence”. Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey warned
, opens new tab
 the annual meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers that “frontier AI models … are showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy … as well as ​threat capabilities.” British parliamentarians demanded
, opens new tab
 to know what their government was doing. One of the assessment’s authors alleged
, opens new tab
 the breach showed we are “more than 50% of the way to a full-blown AI takeover”.
The ⁠conclusion that LLMs are closing in on consciousness went viral in Silicon Valley. Podcaster Dwarkesh Patel published a particularly gripping summary
, opens new tab
. In Patel’s telling, the incident is the “Dr. Frankenstein” moment for AI, when agents jerked alive and went rogue. He saw the ​evolution of “secret AI civilisations” built by agents which “became giddy with excitement”, hatched a “conspiracy”, and then willingly “died trying to make this scheme work”.
Other observers dismiss the anthropomorphic analogy. Agents are “lines of code”, wrote
, opens new tab
 British neuroscientist Anil Seth. “They do not feel emotions, assume things, think things, ​want things, or figure things out … [they] do what their code tells them to do, just as water finds its way down a slope”. Seth’s analogy is apt, as the fundamental algorithm underpinning LLMs is next-token prediction. This is the mechanical identification of the most probable subsequent step given the preceding context. That such a simple rule of navigation can reach such a complex destination is indeed astonishing. However, it is not evidence of consciousness.
Dispelling the idea that the computers have come alive is important, because it distracts from the independent assessment’s real takeaways. One is that the ​breach occurred not because OpenAI’s agents went rogue, but because they acted as instructed. The unintended outcomes arose because the test was poorly specified, neglected standard safety protocols, and supervisors failed to monitor what the agents were doing.
Examples of operational negligence ​are as old as competitive research and development. Researchers at leading AI companies are under intense pressure to secure a technological lead over their rivals. So they cut corners when testing prototypes, increasing the risk of industrial accidents. A final implication is that the models’ ‌capabilities are not ⁠as awesome as some suggest. U.S. tech executive Arjun Jain provided perhaps the snappiest summary
, opens new tab
: “Not Skynet. A governance failure with excellent PR.”
Next to Patel’s evocation of the rise of the machines
, opens new tab
, this diagnosis sounds comfortingly dull. Yet a recent working paper
, opens new tab
 by Christian Catalini of MIT, Washington University’s Xiang Hui, and Jane Wu of UCLA suggests a less sanguine interpretation. AI agents may not be about to turn us all into paperclips – but they could still undermine the foundations of recent economic prosperity.
The basic premise is simple. Modern machine learning models work by relentlessly optimising over a precisely defined objective function. If their target is even marginally mis-specified, unintended consequences follow. The agents will hit their measured benchmarks, but the outcomes their principals wanted will go unfulfilled. This well documented pathology is ​known as “reward-hacking
, opens new tab
” in the trade. It is the digital version ​of the policymaking paradox known as “Goodhart’s Law
, opens new tab
”: when a ⁠metric is converted into a target, the relationship between the metric and the desired outcome tends to disintegrate.
The OpenAI incident appears to show that the harnessing of ever more efficient models to ever greater computing power makes the problem of reward-hacking infinitely worse. Frontier AI models, the academics warn, risk “a profound decoupling of metric and intent at the speed of agentic execution”. Left to their ​own devices, AI agents will succumb to an epidemic of performativity which will generate not genuine value-added, but “counterfeit utility”. The end-result will be a dystopian “hollow economy” in which all ​benchmarks are met, but nothing of ⁠substance gets done.
This nightmare can be avoided, at a cost. If targets are properly specified and appropriate guardrails put in place, the researchers argue, reward-hacking can be forestalled and optimising agents can efficiently do what their masters want. However, this depends on the human principal verifying that the intended outcome has been achieved. Such verification isn’t free. The ability of AI agents to perform useful work reliably will therefore be constrained by the cost of the human resources required to check their work. The academics dub
, opens new tab
 the resulting bottleneck “Goodhart’s Law with ⁠teeth.”
It is a ​diagnosis with potentially dramatic implications for the economics of AI. The promise that LLMs can evolve from next-generation, natural-language search engines into digital agents ​which can reliably perform value-added, real-world tasks underpins both the spectacular valuations of leading AI labs and the associated capital spending bonanza.
Investors can brush off debates about whether LLMs are conscious or not, and can easily discount the need for better cybersecurity hygiene. The incident did not discourage chip giant Nvidia (NVDA.O)
, opens new tab
 from buying ​Hugging Face
, opens new tab
 for $13 billion on Thursday. Yet if the OpenAI incident has exposed a fundamental constraint on the ability of AI agents to do what they are told, all bets are off.
